To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

insulin signaling is differentially regulated during hibernation in the forebrain, cerebellar, and brainstem regions of the ground squirrel brain and that this regulation is associated with the regulation of mitochondrial substrate utilization.
the insulin signaling pathway is differentially regulated in the brain during hibernation in thirteen-lined ground squirlets, and that the regulation of this pathway is region-specific.

insulin signaling is differentially regulated across brain regions in ground squirrels, that the phosphorylation of GSK3 is up-regulated in the brain of ground squirrels during deep torpor and that pyruvate oxidation in the brain of these animals is up-regulated during both deep torpo and interbout arousal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of hibernation, a unique state of mammalian hypothermic torpor, and the role of the insulin signaling pathway in the brain of a hibernating animal.
understanding how hibernation affects brain metabolism and function.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate the insulin signaling pathway in the brain of the thirteen-lined ground squirrel.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the insulin signaling pathway is altered in the brain of torpid ground squirrels, with a specific role of GSK3 in the control of metabolism and apoptosis.
the brain of hibernate ground squirrels has a unique metabolic state that is regulated in a region-specific manner and may be a key factor for their ability to withstand ischemia and hypoxia.
hibernation in the thirteen-lined ground squirrel is characterized by an increase in insulin signaling in the forebrain, a decrease in the cerebellar forebrain, and an increase in the brain stem.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the brain of hiberating ground squirrels is able to maintain glucose homeostasis during periods of extreme energy conservation, and that the brain is able to maintain its metabolic machinery in a ready state to rapidly respond to changes in the environment.

insulin signaling and mitochondrial substrate oxidation are tightly regulated during hibernation and that these processes are likely to be controlled by the phosphoprotein abundance and activity of Akt, GSK3β, and pyruvate carboxylase.

the brain is able to maintain normal metabolic activity in the face of low oxygen delivery by utilizing a variety of metabolic pathways, and that insulin signaling is a crucial component to the metabolic response of the brain during hibernation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain of hiberating squirrels is highly adaptable to changes in metabolic demand, and this adaptation is likely mediated by changes in the activity of the Akt and GSK3β pathways.
insulin signaling is not required for survival of brain tissue during hibernation but may be involved in the recovery from torpor.
the insulin signaling cascade is active in the brains of hibernating animals and is regulated regionally.
